newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: RESEARCH ALERT-No forex controls for Malaysia-IDEA.
newsitem.headline: RESEARCH ALERT-No forex controls for Malaysia-IDEA.

text.p: Malaysia financial markets were on Thursday awashed with rumours the central bank may impose capital controls to prevent a Thai-like crisis, but research house I.D.E.A. doubted any such measure was afoot.

"...Fearing that of a crisis a la Thailand, the market was consumed with talk that Malaysia may be implementing Singapore's kind of FX (foreign exchange) controls, that is imposing a ceiling on the amount of ringgit loans to non-residents.
"But we seriously doubt if BNM (Bank Negara Malaysia) would do that," the Singapore-based firm said in a commentary.
Rumours of the capital control measures gained ground following widespread speculation that Bank Negara was to meet with senior bankers on Thursday or Friday.
Officials at the central bank were not immediately available for comment on both rumours.
Banking sources gave Reuters a mixed response to the supposed meeting, with one saying he was not aware of any meeting involving the central bank.
Another source said the meeting, which he said would take place on Thursday, was to discuss "housekeeping" matters.
I.D.E.A. said that the meetings would be spread over three days beginning on Thursday.
It said Malaysia was unlike Thailand as Kuala Lumpur's economic fundamentals have improved over the last two years.

Malaysia's economic growth has been brought down to a more sustainable level of 8.2 percent last year from 9.5 percent in 1995. Its current account gap has fallen to some 5.5 percent of gross domestic product from 8.8 percent in 1995.
"Although this is still relatively high in the regional context, inflows are well enough -- largely FDI (foreign direct investments -- to finance the country's account gap," it said.

Malaysia plans to start more financial tools in the form of more futures contracts and an over-the-counter market for high-technology stocks, moves which I.D.E.A said preclude any plans to start capital control measures.
It said any move to limit offshore borrowings of the ringgit would create a two-tier market, one for domestic players and another for foreign ones.
"Certainly this will ensure that ringgit falls into the right hands.
"But this will drastically reduce liquidity for offshore in terms of hedging facilities, thereby digging graves for the upcoming financial instruments," the report said.
